references.text: Moses answers the people's fear and cry to the Lord by urging them not to be afraid, but to trust in the Lord's salvation.
Pharaoh's army and chariots that pursued Israel are mentioned in Moses' song of praise after crossing the Red Sea.
Joshua reminds the people how they cried out to the Lord when the Egyptians pursued them by the sea.
Nehemiah refers to how God saw the distress of their ancestors at the Red Sea and heard their cry.
The psalm describes how the ancestors did not understand God's wonders in Egypt and were disobedient at the Red Sea, but God saved them for the sake of His name.
A parallel to how people in distress cry out to the Lord, and He delivers them from their troubles.
An earlier example of the children of Israel groaning and crying out to God during their oppression in Egypt.
The Letter to the Hebrews mentions the faith that led the Israelites to walk through the Red Sea, while the Egyptians who pursued them drowned.
Direct continuation of the same event: a shift from fear of the enemy (v.10) to fear of and trust in the Lord after salvation (v.31).
Thematic parallel: The people's faith and worship as a response to God seeing their distress (before the Exodus versus at the Red Sea).
Theological parallel: God's response to Israel's 'cry' and that He sees their oppression.
Contrasting parallel: The direction of fear reverses; in 14:10 Israel fears the enemy, while in Numbers 22 the enemy fears Israel.
Theological pattern: Israel's reaction to oppression is to cry out to the Lord for help.
Thematic parallel: The enemy's attack leads people to cry out to the Lord for help.
